summary.text: Reading from the least significant coefficient upward, the proof replaces each signed coefficient together with a carry in \(\{0,-1\}\) by a digit in \(\{0,1,b-2,b-1\}\) and a new carry in \(\{0,-1\}\); a geometric bound on an \(n\)-digit base-\(b\) number rules out a terminal carry of \(-1\) after choosing the sign of the whole sum to make it nonnegative. Thus the absolute value has such a positional representation, and repeated quotient–remainder extraction shows that all of its base-\(b\) digits are among those four values (with the omitted zeroth power contributing only a trailing zero).

full_proof.text:
Let \(b\ge 5\), and let \(n\ge 0\). We prove the claim for an arbitrary assignment of signs to the powers \(b,b^2,\ldots,b^n\). Thus let
\[
X=\sum_{k=1}^n \sigma_k b^k,
\qquad \sigma_k\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
The prime-dependent signs defining A243106 are one particular choice of the \(\sigma_k\), so the result for arbitrary signs includes that sequence.

We will first prove a more general signed-digit normalization result for powers beginning with \(b^0\).

**Carry-normalization lemma.** Suppose \(\varepsilon_0,\ldots,\varepsilon_{m-1}\in\{1,-1\}\), and suppose an incoming carry \(c\) is either \(0\) or \(-1\). Then there are digits
\[
a_0,\ldots,a_{m-1}\in\{0,1,b-2,b-1\}
\]
and a terminal carry \(C\in\{0,-1\}\) such that
\[
c+\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\varepsilon_k b^k
 =\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}a_kb^k+Cb^m. \tag{1}
\]
Moreover, every \(a_k\) is a legitimate base-\(b\) digit, i.e. \(0\le a_k<b\).

We prove this by induction on \(m\). When \(m=0\), there are no digits to choose, and taking \(C=c\) gives (1).

Now suppose there are \(m+1\) signed digits. At the units place, the sum of the incoming carry and the signed coefficient is
\[
t=c+\varepsilon_0.
\]
Because \(c\in\{0,-1\}\) and \(\varepsilon_0\in\{1,-1\}\), there are exactly four possibilities. In each case write \(t=a_0+c'b\) as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
t&a_0&c'\\ \hline
1&1&0\\
0&0&0\\
-1&b-1&-1\\
-2&b-2&-1.
\end{array}
\]
Thus \(a_0\in\{0,1,b-2,b-1\}\) and the outgoing carry \(c'\) is again in \(\{0,-1\}\). Since \(b\ge5\), all four possible values of \(a_0\) lie between \(0\) and \(b-1\).

Apply the induction hypothesis to the remaining signs \(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m\), with incoming carry \(c'\). It supplies digits \(a'_0,\ldots,a'_{m-1}\) of the required kind and a terminal carry \(C\in\{0,-1\}\) such that
\[
c'+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\varepsilon_{j+1}b^j
 =\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a'_jb^j+Cb^m.
\]
Multiplying this identity by \(b\) and using \(c+\varepsilon_0=a_0+c'b\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
c+\sum_{k=0}^{m}\varepsilon_kb^k
 &=c+\varepsilon_0+b\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\varepsilon_{j+1}b^j\\
 &=a_0+b\left(c'+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\varepsilon_{j+1}b^j\right)\\
 &=a_0+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a'_jb^{j+1}+Cb^{m+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking \(a_{j+1}=a'_j\) completes the induction and proves the carry-normalization lemma.

We next record the bound that rules out a nonzero terminal carry when the normalized number is nonnegative.

**Digit-value bound.** If \(0\le a_k<b\) for \(0\le k<m\), then
\[
0\le A:=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}a_kb^k<b^m. \tag{2}
\]
The lower bound is immediate. For completeness, the strict upper bound follows by induction on \(m\). It is clear for \(m=0\), where the sum is zero and \(b^0=1\). For \(m+1\), separate the least significant digit:
\[
A=a_0+bA',
\qquad
A'=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a_{j+1}b^j.
\]
By induction, \(A'<b^m\), hence, since these are integers, \(A'\le b^m-1\). Also \(a_0\le b-1\). Consequently
\[
A\le (b-1)+b(b^m-1)=b^{m+1}-1<b^{m+1}.
\]
This proves (2).

Now consider any normalized signed sum
\[
V=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\varepsilon_kb^k,
\qquad \varepsilon_k\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
We claim that there are legitimate digits \(a_k\in\{0,1,b-2,b-1\}\) such that
\[
|V|=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}a_kb^k. \tag{3}
\]

First suppose \(V\ge0\). Apply the carry-normalization lemma with incoming carry \(c=0\). It gives
\[
V=A+Cb^m,
\qquad A=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}a_kb^k,
\qquad C\in\{0,-1\}.
\]
If \(C=-1\), then (2) yields
\[
V=A-b^m<0,
\]
contrary to \(V\ge0\). Therefore \(C=0\), so \(V=A\), and hence \(|V|=A\).

If \(V<0\), replace every sign \(\varepsilon_k\) by \(-\varepsilon_k\). These are still signs in \(\{1,-1\}\), and their signed sum is \(-V>0\). Applying the preceding argument to \(-V\) gives digits of the required kind with
\[
-V=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}a_kb^k.
\]
Since \(|V|=-V\), this again proves (3).

It remains to justify that the coefficients in (3) really control every digit in the ordinary base-\(b\) expansion, including when some high coefficients vanish. We use the following elementary fact.

**Digit-extraction lemma.** Let
\[
A=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}a_kb^k
\]
with \(0\le a_k<b\), and assume \(b\ge2\). Then every digit occurring in the usual base-\(b\) expansion of \(A\) is equal to one of \(a_0,\ldots,a_{m-1}\).

This is proved by induction on \(m\). For \(m=0\), \(A=0\); under the convention that the digit list of zero is empty there is nothing to prove, while under the convention that zero is written as the single digit \(0\), the desired conclusion in our application is immediate because \(0\) is allowed. For the induction step, write
\[
A=a_0+bA',
\qquad A'=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a_{j+1}b^j.
\]
If \(A=0\), again there is nothing substantive to prove. If \(A>0\), the least significant base-\(b\) digit is \(A\bmod b\), and the remaining digit string is the base-\(b\) expansion of \(\lfloor A/b\rfloor\). Because \(0\le a_0<b\),
\[
A\bmod b=a_0,
\qquad
\left\lfloor\frac A b\right\rfloor=A'.
\]
Thus the first digit is \(a_0\), and every remaining digit is, by induction applied to \(A'\), one of \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). This proves the lemma.

We now return to the original sum over the first \(n\) positive powers. Define
\[
V=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\sigma_{j+1}b^j.
\]
Reindexing the original sum and factoring out one power of \(b\) gives
\[
X=\sum_{k=1}^n\sigma_kb^k
  =b\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\sigma_{j+1}b^j
  =bV. \tag{4}
\]
By (3), there are digits
\[
a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}\in\{0,1,b-2,b-1\}
\]
with
\[
|V|=A:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_jb^j.
\]
As \(b>0\), equation (4) implies
\[
|X|=b|V|=bA. \tag{5}
\]

If \(A=0\), then \(|X|=0\), whose only possible displayed digit is \(0\), so the assertion holds. If \(A>0\), multiplication by \(b\) shifts a base-\(b\) expansion one place to the left. Equivalently, the least significant digit of \(bA\) is
\[
(bA)\bmod b=0,
\]
and division by \(b\) leaves \(A\). Hence the digits of \(|X|=bA\) consist of a final least-significant \(0\), together with the digits of \(A\). The digit-extraction lemma shows that every digit of \(A\) is one of the coefficients \(a_j\), and each such coefficient belongs to
\[
\{0,1,b-2,b-1\}.
\]
The added least-significant digit \(0\) belongs to the same set. Therefore every base-\(b\) digit of \(|X|\) is one of
\[
0,\quad 1,\quad b-2,\quad b-1.
\]
This holds for every \(b\ge5\), every \(n\), and every independent assignment of signs to the first \(n\) positive powers of \(b\), as required.
